message.content: I heard that near the Egyptian Naucratis there lived one of the ancient gods of that place, to whom was consecrated a bird called the ibis. The name of this deity — Teut[172]. He first invented number, arithmetic, geometry and astronomy, the game of draughts and dice, and invented [107]also letters as well. The king of all Egypt at that time was D. Famus[173], who sat in a large city of the upper part of the country. This city the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and the god — Ammon. Once Teut, having come to Famus, announced to him about his arts and said that it was necessary to communicate them to all the Egyptians; but the latter asked him: what use can each of them provide? When Teut began to explain this, — the king, depending on whether the explanation appeared to him good or bad, censured some things and praised others. In general, he said much to Teut E. about each art in the one and the other direction: to relate about this would be long. Finally the matter came to letters, and Teut said: Sovereign! this science will make the Egyptians wiser and more mindful; I invented it as a means for memory and wisdom. But the king answered: Much-learned Teut! one is able to give birth to arts, and another to judge how much harm or profit they will bring to the people who will make use of them. Here you, father of letters, from 275. parental love, have ascribed to them the opposite of what they can. For this, weakening the carefulness about remembering, will produce in the souls of the pupils forgetfulness[174]; because, relying on external writing, depicted by foreign signs, they will not recall impressions internally — themselves in [108]themselves. So, you invented a means not for remembering, but for reminding. And wisdom too the pupils will acquire[175] from you not true, but seeming; because having listened to much and studying nothing, they will represent themselves as knowers of many things and, as supposed sages, instead of true ones, B. will remain for the most part ignorant and people in society insufferable.
message.reasoning:
I need to translate this literally into English while preserving the structural markers like Stephanus numbers and footnote references, keeping them in place without adding anything extra. I'm starting with the passage about the ancient god near Egyptian Naucratis associated with the ibis bird.

The deity's name was Teut, who invented number, arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, games like draughts and dice, and also letters. I'm continuing with how the Egyptian king at that time — rendered as Famus, seated in the great upper city the Greeks call Thebes, with the god called Ammon — received Teut, who came and presented his various arts and inventions.

Famus questioned the usefulness of each art Teut presented, praising or criticizing them according to his judgment, until the discussion reached letters, where Teut argued this invention would make the Egyptians wiser and strengthen their memory, since he devised it as a remedy for memory and wisdom.

The king disputed this, replying that the inventor of an art isn't necessarily the best judge of its real benefit or harm to those who use it, suggesting that Teut's fatherly affection for letters led him to see the opposite of their true effect. He reasoned that relying on written symbols would weaken people's internal effort to remember, since they'd depend on external signs rather than recalling impressions from within themselves.
